title: 道德經 第四十七章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 47, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 76. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 47 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 鑒遠 (Surveying the Distant). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
不出戶，
知天下；
不闚牖，
見天道。

morph.gloss: to go out, to step outside
the single-leaf door of a room (the double gate is 門)
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it
to peep, to squint through at — a rare graph for 窺
a window, the latticed opening in a wall
jiàn: to see, to look upon
way, course — 天道 is heaven's way, the regular course of things

sentences.l:
Not going out the door — know all under heaven;
not peeping through the window — see heaven's way.
sentences.i: Without going out the door, one may know all under heaven; without peering through the window, one may see the way of heaven.
sentences.n:
Four bare verb phrases, two to a pair, with no subject, no 'if' and no 'then'. The first of each pair is the condition and the second the consequence, and nothing on the page says so — the arrangement says it. English cannot be that bare, which is why the literal has to put in a dash.

戶 and 牖 are the two openings of a house: the door of a single room and the window. Naming both is the classical way of saying 'without leaving the house at all' — one does not even go as far as the window.

天道 stays two words here, as 常道 did in chapter 1: it is modifier plus noun, heaven's way, meaning just what its parts mean — the course heaven runs, the regularity of things. Wang Bi's comment is the chapter's argument in miniature: affairs have an ancestor and things have a ruler, the roads differ but the destination is one, so from where you stand you may know the beginning of things.

sentences.t:
其出彌遠，
其知彌少。

morph.gloss: his, one's — with nobody named, it generalises: whoever does it
going out — the verb standing as a noun
knowing — again a verb standing as a noun

sentences.l:
His going out ever farther,
his knowing ever less.
sentences.i: The farther afield he goes, the less he knows.
sentences.n:
彌 … 彌 … is the correlative: 'the more … the more …'. Each clause puts 彌 in front of its adjective and the two clauses are simply set side by side; nothing marks the link, and there is no 'than' anywhere. English needs 'the … the …' to say it at all.

其 in front of a verb makes a noun of it — 其出 'his going out', 其知 'his knowing' — the same trick as 其已 'his stopping' back in chapter 9. And 其 here belongs to nobody in particular: no subject has been named, so it means whoever does this.

Wang Bi is blunt about why: if you know it, you have no need to go out; if you do not know it, then the farther out you go the more lost you get.

sentences.t:
是以聖人不行而知，
不見而名，

morph.gloss: therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither half gives you it alone
the sage — in this book the ruler who holds the Way, not a moral saint
xíng: to walk, to travel, to go about
and yet, but — joining two predicates of one subject
jiàn: to see, to look at
to name — the noun 'name' used as a verb: to put a name to a thing

sentences.l:
Therefore the sage does not travel, and yet knows;
does not look, and yet names.
sentences.i: So the sage knows without travelling and names without looking.
sentences.n:
而 is doing the adversative here — 'and yet' — tying two predicates onto one subject. 不行而知 is four characters for a whole sentence: does-not-travel and-yet knows.

名 is the noun 'a name' pressed into service as a verb, 'to name', with nothing marking the change. That is Wang Bi's reading and the reason it stands here: knowing what things come from, he says, one can put a name to the pattern of right and wrong without having seen the case. 名 and 明 míng 'clear-sighted' are homophones in Mandarin and are written for each other all over early texts, and this line has been read both ways. Wang Bi's text has 名 and his comment takes it as naming, so 名 is what stands here — the claim being not that the sage sees anyway, but that he can say what a thing is without having looked.

morph.gloss: wéi: to do, to act — with no object at all
to complete, to bring to fulfilment; to come to completion

sentences.l: Does not act, and yet completes.
sentences.i: He does not act, and the thing is brought to completion.
sentences.n:
Four characters, and the chapter's whole point. 為 stands here with no object — the bare verb 'to act' — so the line restates 無為, acting without forcing, without using the term.

成 can be read either way and Chinese does not choose: he completes it, or it comes to completion. The ambiguity is the sense, since what the line denies is that the completing is his doing.
